D01.title: Overview of the analysable evidence base: included urban shotgun metagenomes and separately held food-related contextual samples
D01.interpretation: The evidence base comprised 8,053 included urban environmental metagenomes from 112 datasets, 122 repository projects, 106 reported countries and 274 source-labelled cities, together with 840 food-related contextual samples from 16 datasets. Availability contracted sharply with each annotation layer: 6,134 urban samples had coordinates, 1,072 had any gene-level AMR table (447 CARD/RGI; 625 ResFinder/KMA) and only 447 had a taxonomic table; the CARD/RGI profiles came from a single dataset (Table R09u). Collection years spanned 2011-2026 among the 7,375 samples with a reported year. Of the food-related samples, 155 had ResFinder/KMA tables. Most samples therefore contributed metadata only. The counts describe repository availability, not sampling intensity or representativeness, and the two AMR pipelines are not interchangeable.
D01.notes: Samples = included public shotgun metagenomes. Cities = distinct source-reported City|Country pairs. AMR and taxonomy tables are producer-processed. Food-related samples are contextual and never pooled with urban samples. Descriptive counts; no statistical test.

D02.title: Included urban samples by sample type: dataset, country and city coverage, annotation availability and repository-reported sequencing depth
D02.interpretation: Municipal wastewater contributed the most samples (2,254; 28.0%) and the widest geographic coverage (35 datasets, 104 countries, 243 cities), followed by transit surfaces (1,911; 23.7%) from only 4 datasets and built environments (1,449; 18.0%). Hospital wastewater was the smallest type (237; 2.9%). Median depth ranged from 0.22 Gbp in hospital wastewater (IQR 0.05-4.03) to 10.51 Gbp in municipal wastewater and 10.71 Gbp in urban soil; surface water was the most heterogeneous (IQR 0.04-14.86 Gbp; SD of log10 bases 1.60), whereas community wastewater was uniform (SD 0.15). Taxonomic tables existed only for community wastewater (447 of 529). Depth differences of this size can alter gene detection independently of biology, so sample-type contrasts require depth adjustment.
D02.notes: pct = share of 8,053 included samples. Depth = total sequenced bases from repository run records (Gbp, 10^9 bases), not post-QC depth; Q1/Q3 = quartiles. Cities counted only where source-labelled. Descriptive; no test.

D04.title: Included urban samples by reported country and continent, with numbers of sample types, cities, datasets and AMR-annotated samples
D04.interpretation: Samples came from 106 countries, but contributions were highly uneven: the United States (1,051), China (1,043), the United Kingdom (821), India (642) and Hong Kong (497) led, 15 countries contributed at least 100 samples and 48 contributed fewer than 10. AMR-table availability was decoupled from sample numbers: India had 451 AMR-annotated samples, China 2 and the United Kingdom none, and 42 countries had no AMR-annotated sample. Bangladesh contributed 18 samples across 4 sample types and 4 datasets, none with a producer-processed AMR table, and Pakistan 13 (2 with AMR tables). The 269 samples without a reported continent (Table D05) are not listed. Counts reflect deposition and project design, not national AMR burden, and do not support country ranking.
D04.notes: Country and continent as reported by the source (Hong Kong listed separately; Mauritius under open ocean). cities = source-labelled cities; with_AMR = samples with a producer-processed CARD/RGI or ResFinder/KMA table. Descriptive counts; no test.

D05.title: Cross-tabulation of included urban samples by continent and sample type
D05.interpretation: Asia contributed 3,088 samples, Europe 2,066, North America 1,429, Africa 845, South America 220 and Oceania 130; 269 lacked a reported continent and 6 were assigned to the open ocean. Sample-type composition differed strongly between continents. Asia supplied 1,042 of 1,449 built-environment and 453 of 529 community-wastewater samples, Europe the largest share of municipal wastewater (867 of 2,254), and North America most surface-water samples (529 of 882). Transit surfaces came mainly from North America (655) and Europe (654). Africa had no air or surface-water samples, and South America and Oceania had no air or built-environment samples. Because continent and sample type were jointly structured by a few projects, any continental contrast would mix matrix and study effects.
D05.notes: Cells = numbers of included samples; continent as reported or derived from the source country. Descriptive cross-tabulation; no statistical test.

D06.title: Included urban samples by source-labelled city, with sample types, contributing datasets and AMR- and taxonomy-annotated samples
D06.interpretation: The 274 source-labelled cities were dominated by single-project contributions: London (531) and New York City (423) were transit-surface samples from one dataset, and Mumbai (189), Chennai (109), Delhi (100) and Kolkata (49) were community-wastewater samples from DS02, the only cities with taxonomic tables. Of the remaining labels, 237 came from the global sewage dataset alone (223 of them with 8 or fewer samples), and 67 cities had a single sample. Only 79 cities had any AMR-annotated sample, and 6 spanned more than one sample type. Dhaka appeared with 8 labelled samples because DS84 samples lacked a source city label (Table GI06). Labels are source-reported and include spelling variants and occasional inconsistent country assignments, so counts are approximate and do not support city ranking.
D06.notes: City = source-reported City|Country pair, not standardized; spelling variants (e.g., Kochi/Cochin) are listed separately. with_AMR and with_taxonomy = samples with producer-processed tables. 5,069 samples without a City|Country pair are excluded (Table D07). Descriptive counts.

D07.title: Summary of city coverage in the included evidence base and its implications for the proposal's multi-city framing
D07.interpretation: Although 274 source-labelled cities were represented, coverage was thin: 33 cities had at least 10 samples, 12 had at least 30, 67 had a single sample and the median was 3 samples per city (IQR 2-5). Only 6 cities were represented in more than one sample type, 79 had at least one AMR-annotated sample and 4 had a taxonomy-annotated sample, while 5,069 included samples lacked a usable City|Country pair. The table implies that the number of city labels exceeded the proposal's target, but a comparable multi-city analysis was not feasible: city-level inference was restricted to the DS02 Indian cities and to uniformly reprocessed South Asian runs. Because most cities were sampled in one matrix by one project, city and matrix effects cannot be separated.
D07.notes: City = source-reported City|Country pair. AMR- and taxonomy-annotated = at least one producer-processed table. Samples lacking a pair had a missing city or a missing or unverified country. Descriptive counts; IQR = interquartile range.

D09.title: Sequencing platform family by sample type among included urban samples
D09.interpretation: Illumina platforms produced 7,002 of the 8,053 included samples, followed by DNBSEQ/MGI/BGISEQ (690), Oxford Nanopore (343), Ion Torrent (12) and PacBio (6). All air, community-wastewater and transit-surface samples were Illumina. Long-read data were concentrated in a few matrices: 311 of the 343 Nanopore samples were surface water and 32 hospital wastewater, and Ion Torrent and PacBio occurred only in municipal wastewater. DNBSEQ-family data came mainly from municipal wastewater (297) and built environments (261). Platform was therefore partly confounded with sample type, notably for surface water, in which 311 of 882 samples were Nanopore. Because read length and error profiles affect alignment-based gene detection, any reanalysis of raw reads across matrices would require platform stratification or sensitivity analysis.
D09.notes: Platform family from repository run metadata. Cells = numbers of included samples. Descriptive cross-tabulation; no statistical test.

D12.title: Availability of coordinates, AMR gene tables, taxonomic tables and diversity indices by sample type among included urban samples
D12.interpretation: Coordinates were available for 6,134 samples (76.2%), ranging from 15.5% of community-wastewater and 32.5% of hospital-wastewater samples to 94.8% of built-environment samples. Gene-level AMR tables covered 1,072 samples (13.3%) and were strongly matrix-specific: CARD/RGI tables existed only for community wastewater (447; 84.5%), ResFinder/KMA tables mainly for municipal wastewater (522; 23.2%), and no other type exceeded 5.6%. Urban soil and hospital wastewater had no producer-processed AMR table. Taxonomic tables were restricted to community wastewater (5.6% overall). The table implies that annotation database was aligned with matrix, so CARD- and ResFinder-based results cannot be compared without confounding, which is why the streams were analysed separately and hospital wastewater was analysable only after reprocessing.
D12.notes: Percentages use the samples of each type as denominator. AMR = producer-processed CARD/RGI or ResFinder/KMA gene table; diversity = producer-provided diversity indices. Descriptive counts; no test.

GI06.title: Proposal target cities (Delhi, Dhaka, Karachi): included datasets, producer-processed AMR and taxonomy coverage, and runs uniformly reprocessed in this update
GI06.interpretation: Delhi was the only target city with producer-processed resistome and taxonomic tables: 100 DS02 community-wastewater samples (2022-2024), of which 12 runs were also uniformly reprocessed. Its other included samples (90 built-environment, 10 air and two single river-sediment samples) had no AMR tables. Dhaka was represented by DS01 municipal sewage (4 samples, 2017-2018), DS03 hospital and community wastewater (4, 2025) and DS84 hospital, municipal and surface-water samples (8, 2024), none with producer-processed AMR tables; all were uniformly reprocessed, and DS84 samples carried no source city label. Karachi had 8 DS01 samples (2016-2018), one with a ResFinder/KMA table and 7 reprocessed runs. Dhaka and Karachi were therefore analysable only through reprocessing, with small samples and Dhaka matrix confounded with dataset and year.
GI06.notes: samples = included samples per dataset and sample type; reprocessed runs are counted per dataset and repeated across its rows. Uniform pipeline: fastp, Kraken 2/SILVA 16S, KMA/ResFinder. Descriptive inventory; no test.

R09u.title: Inventory of the 112 datasets with included urban samples: sample types, countries, verified corrections, recovered site identifiers, AMR profiles and reprocessed runs
R09u.interpretation: The 112 datasets varied greatly in size. Three contributed most samples: MetaSUB transit surfaces (DS04; 1,804), the global sewage programme (DS01; 1,034) and DS02 Indian open drains (447), whereas 32 datasets had fewer than 10 samples and only 14 had at least 100. CARD/RGI profiles came from DS02 alone (447), and ResFinder/KMA profiles from 15 datasets, chiefly DS01 (315), DS20 (69) and DS18 (60). Site identifiers were recovered only for DS02 (19 sites), and sample types were corrected for 4 DS84 samples. Runs reprocessed in this update came from DS01 (27), DS02 (12), DS84 (8) and DS03 (4). Seven datasets spanned more than one sample type. Pooled sample counts therefore overweight a few projects, and dataset is the relevant unit for between-study heterogeneity.
R09u.notes: included_samples = included urban shotgun metagenomes. Country lists may be truncated in the source field; two datasets lacked a verified country. Profiles = producer-processed gene tables; reprocessed runs = uniform-pipeline runs. Descriptive inventory.

S01.title: Coverage of the global sample map: included samples with and without source-reported coordinates, distinct locations and coordinate-country mismatches
S01.interpretation: Of the 8,053 included samples, 6,134 had source-reported coordinates and were mapped, while 1,919 lacked coordinates and could not be placed. The mapped samples shared only 2,557 distinct coordinate pairs, indicating repeated sampling at the same locations and frequent use of site- or city-level coordinates rather than unique sample positions. A further 228 samples had coordinates lying more than 25 km from their reported country; these were mapped as reported and flagged rather than corrected. The map therefore shows where samples were reported to originate, with uneven positional precision, and was not used to interpolate surfaces or estimate prevalence. Point density reflects sampling effort and repository deposition, not resistance risk.
S01.notes: Coordinates as reported by the source; no geocoding of place names. Mismatch = coordinate more than 25 km from the reported country's territory. Counts of included samples; descriptive.

S03.title: Country coverage by ISO code: included urban samples, number of sample types and samples with producer-processed AMR tables
S03.interpretation: The table lists 106 countries by ISO code. Breadth of matrix coverage was limited: only 4 countries (US, CN, GB and IN) were represented in 6 sample types, while 68 contributed a single type. AMR-table availability did not follow sample numbers. The United States had 75 AMR-annotated samples of 1,051, China 2 of 1,043 and the United Kingdom (GB) none of 821, whereas India had 451 of 642, reflecting the single DS02 dataset. Of the 106 countries, 42 had no AMR-annotated sample, and in 4 small contributors (ZM, MD, GM and XK) every sample had an AMR table. Mapped AMR coverage therefore reflects which projects deposited processed tables, not geographic differences in resistance, and countries with zero AMR tables are data gaps rather than evidence of absence.
S03.notes: ISO2 = ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code (XK = Kosovo, user-assigned; HK listed separately). with_AMR_table = samples with a producer-processed CARD/RGI or ResFinder/KMA table. Descriptive counts; no test.

SA01.title: Sensitivity of DS02 city fold changes in total normalized ARG abundance relative to Delhi across seven sample-level model specifications
SA01.interpretation: In the primary specification, total normalized ARG abundance was lower than in Delhi for Chennai (fold change 0.61), Mumbai (0.62) and Kolkata (0.81). All 21 estimates remained below 1 across the seven specifications. Restricting hits to allele coverage of at least 80% lowered the ratios (Chennai 0.54, Mumbai 0.55, Kolkata 0.70), whereas normalizing by prokaryote-classified reads attenuated the Chennai and Mumbai contrasts to 0.77 and 0.79. Excluding depth-flagged samples (n = 443), adjusting for taxonomic cluster, or using 96 city-month geometric means changed estimates little (e.g., Chennai 0.61, Mumbai 0.62, Kolkata 0.80 for city-month means). Because these are sample-level models of repeated monthly samples from few sites, the confidence intervals and p-values are too narrow; only the direction of effects is informative.
SA01.notes: Fold change = back-transformed OLS coefficient of log total abundance versus Delhi, adjusted for season and year, with HC3 robust errors. RPKM = reads per kilobase per million sequenced reads (primary). n = samples or city-months. Site-aware tests are primary.

SA02.title: Sensitivity of the DS02 city effect on total normalized ARG abundance (Kruskal-Wallis epsilon-squared) across six sample-level specifications
SA02.interpretation: The sample-level city effect was moderate in the primary specification (H = 91.9, n = 447, epsilon-squared 0.20) and nearly unchanged when hits were restricted to allele coverage of at least 50% (0.21) or 80% (0.20), or when depth-flagged samples were excluded (0.21; n = 443). Normalizing by prokaryote-classified reads reduced the effect to 0.06 (H = 31.2), indicating that part of the apparent city difference in RPKM may reflect differences in the prokaryotic fraction of sequenced reads. Aggregating to 96 city-month geometric means gave 0.33. The city effect was present under every specification, but its magnitude was denominator-sensitive. Repeated monthly samples of the same sites are not independent, so these p-values are descriptive and only the direction of effects is informative.
SA02.notes: Kruskal-Wallis test of total normalized ARG abundance across four cities; epsilon-squared = H-based effect size. Unit = sample (or city-month). RPKM = reads per kilobase per million sequenced reads. Primary inference uses site-aware tests.

SA03.title: Sensitivity of ResFinder matrix and food-related contrasts in total normalized ARG abundance to project duplication, KMA version, denominator and template coverage
SA03.interpretation: In the primary mixed model (396 units, 15 studies), abundance relative to municipal wastewater was lower in built environments (fold change 0.10; 95% CI 0.01-0.68) and surface water (0.23; 0.08-0.69), with wide intervals including 1 for air (0.13; 0.01-1.41) and transit surfaces (0.33; 0.03-3.49); food-related contextual units had 0.24 (0.08-0.67). All 30 estimates remained below 1. Swapping or double-counting the pilot projects changed estimates little. Excluding studies run with KMA 1.2.21 (309 units, 13 studies) strengthened several contrasts, including air (0.14; 0.02-0.97). Normalizing by total trimmed fragments left only built environments with an interval excluding 1 (0.07; 0.005-0.84), and the food-related contrast lost support (0.40; 0.08-1.97). Direction was robust, but statistical support depended on specification, and matrix remains confounded with study.
SA03.notes: Linear mixed models of log total FPKM with a study random intercept; fold change versus municipal wastewater. FPKM = fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments (primary). Units = analysis units of the curated resource; food-related contrast fitted in a separate model.

SA04.title: Sensitivity analysis of ResFinder matrix differences in total normalized ARG abundance using study-level medians as the unit of analysis
SA04.interpretation: When each study-by-matrix combination was reduced to its median, so that studies rather than samples formed the unit of analysis, the Kruskal-Wallis test across 5 matrices did not support a matrix difference (H = 5.42, df = 4, p = 0.25; n = 16 study-matrix units). The effect size (epsilon-squared 0.13) was not negligible, but the test had very low power because most matrices were represented by one to a few studies. This result is consistent with the confounding of matrix with study in the ResFinder resource: the sample-level and mixed-model matrix contrasts (Table SA03) rest heavily on between-study differences. A non-significant result here is not evidence that matrices share the same resistome abundance.
SA04.notes: Unit = study x matrix median of total FPKM (fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments); k = number of matrices; n = study-matrix units. Kruskal-Wallis test; epsilon-squared = H-based effect size.

SA05.title: Additional robustness checks: phylum richness with and without rarefaction, resistome composition under Aitchison distance, and random-forest stability across seeds
SA05.interpretation: Phylum richness in DS02 differed between cities whether observed (H = 24.0; epsilon-squared 0.05) or rarefied (H = 61.8; 0.13), so the city signal was not explained by unequal depth; rarefaction strengthened rather than removed it. Resistome composition also differed by city under Aitchison distance on gene families present in at least 50% of samples (PERMANOVA R-squared 0.11, p = 0.001; n = 447). Model A, a random forest classifying municipal wastewater against other matrices, gave a mean leave-one-study-out ROC-AUC of 0.66 across five seeds (SD 0.007; range 0.646-0.667), indicating stable but modest discrimination. The DS02 checks are sample-level analyses of repeated site samples, so their p-values are descriptive.
SA05.notes: Kruskal-Wallis epsilon-squared for richness; PERMANOVA R-squared for composition (unit = sample). ROC-AUC = area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; LOGO = leave-one-group (study)-out validation; SD across seeds.

SD01.title: Included urban samples by sample type retained at each repository sequencing-depth threshold, used as sensitivity denominators only
SD01.interpretation: Of 8,053 included samples, 7,822 met a 10 Mbp threshold, 7,411 met 100 Mbp, 6,701 met 500 Mbp and 5,840 met 1 Gbp; 642 samples fell below 100 Mbp. Losses were concentrated in particular matrices. At 100 Mbp, surface water lost 260 samples (882 to 622), built environments 171 and hospital wastewater 87 (237 to 150, falling to 78 at 1 Gbp), whereas community wastewater lost 1 and urban soil 3. Transit surfaces were largely retained to 500 Mbp (1,695) but fell to 1,214 at 1 Gbp. Because any depth filter would remove hospital wastewater and surface water disproportionately, thresholds were applied only in sensitivity analyses, not as exclusions. Depth here is total repository bases, not post-QC depth.
SD01.notes: Columns = numbers of included samples with total sequenced bases at or above each threshold (Mbp = 10^6, Gbp = 10^9 bases); lost_at_100Mbp = samples below 100 Mbp. No samples were removed from the primary analysis. Descriptive counts.

SD03.title: DS02 site-aware tests of city differences in resistome metrics at each sequencing-depth threshold (site-level Kruskal-Wallis and mixed-model likelihood-ratio tests)
SD03.interpretation: Site-aware results were identical from no threshold through 500 Mbp because no DS02 sample was removed (447 samples, 19 sites). Total normalized ARG abundance differed between cities (site-level H = 9.87, permutation p = 0.0046; mixed-model LRT p = 0.0007; site ICC 0.11), as did gene-family richness at 50% coverage (H = 13.65, permutation p = 0.0002; LRT p < 0.001). Shannon diversity was not supported by the site-level test (H = 6.97, p = 0.056), although the mixed-model LRT gave p = 0.026. At 1 Gbp, one sample was removed (446) and results were essentially unchanged (abundance H = 10.00, p = 0.004). The analysis shows insensitivity of DS02 conclusions to depth filtering, but it is not a general test of depth robustness because DS02 was uniformly deep.
SD03.notes: Site-level Kruskal-Wallis on 19 site medians with whole-site permutation p-values; mixed-model LRT for city with site random intercept; ICC_site = intraclass correlation for site. RPKM = reads per kilobase per million sequenced reads.

SD04.title: ResFinder study-random-intercept model of total normalized ARG abundance by matrix, as fold change versus municipal wastewater, at each sequencing-depth threshold
SD04.interpretation: Applying depth thresholds reduced the analysed units from 396 to 395 at 100 Mbp, 380 at 500 Mbp and 327 at 1 Gbp, while all 15 studies were retained. All 20 matrix estimates kept the direction of the primary model. Built environments (0.10 without a threshold; 0.10 at 1 Gbp, 95% CI 0.01-0.76) and surface water (0.23; 0.24 at 1 Gbp, 0.08-0.75) had intervals excluding 1 at every threshold, whereas the intervals for air (0.13-0.14) and transit surfaces (0.32-0.34) included 1 throughout. Surface-water units fell from 46 to 30 and transit-surface units from 24 to 19 at 1 Gbp. Matrix estimates were thus insensitive to depth filtering, but they remain confounded with study, and built environments contributed only 9 units.
SD04.notes: Linear mixed model of log total FPKM with study random intercept; fold change versus municipal wastewater (MW). FPKM = fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments. Units = samples; units_in_matrix = units of that matrix retained.

SD05.title: Median genus Shannon diversity, ARG gene richness and total normalized ARG abundance by ResFinder matrix at each sequencing-depth threshold
SD05.interpretation: Without a threshold, municipal wastewater (293 units) had median genus Shannon 4.06, ARG gene richness 89 and total abundance 105,480 FPKM, compared with Shannon 4.88 and richness 53.5 in air, and 3.95 and 60 in built environments. Medians for air and built environments were unchanged at every threshold because all their units were retained. At 1 Gbp, municipal wastewater retained 245 units and its median richness rose to 104 (Shannon 4.13), consistent with depth-dependent gene detection, while abundance was stable (103,028). Surface-water medians shifted irregularly as units were removed (total abundance 31,579, then 41,096 at 500 Mbp and 23,449 at 1 Gbp). These are unadjusted medians whose changes partly reflect which studies were removed, so they describe stability rather than matrix effects.
SD05.notes: Medians per matrix among units retained at each threshold. FPKM = fragments per kilobase per million rRNA-aligned bacterial fragments; gene richness = number of ResFinder genes detected; genus Shannon from rRNA-mapped reads. Descriptive; no test.

SD07.title: Uniformly reprocessed runs: median ARG gene richness by analysis group at successive fractions of the analysed sequencing depth
SD07.interpretation: Median ARG gene richness increased with every increase in analysed depth in all groups, without a plateau. For any hit, Dhaka medians rose from 98.5 at a quarter of the analysed depth to 123.5 at half and 148.5 at full depth; the DS01 comparator rose from 99.0 to 151.0, the calibration unit from 100.5 to 140.5 and the DS02 Delhi open-drain comparator from 73.5 to 110.5. Genes supported by at least two fragments showed the same pattern (Dhaka 66.0 to 109.0; Delhi 49.0 to 82.0). Richness at the analysed depth was therefore not saturated, so gene counts are comparable only at equal depth, as ensured by uniform subsampling, and rare genes are likely under-detected. Groups differ in matrix, study and period.
SD07.notes: Binomial thinning of the uniformly subsampled read pairs; depth_fraction 1.0 = full analysed subsample. genes_any_hit = ResFinder genes with any KMA hit (unconfirmed upper bound); genes_ge2_fragments = genes supported by at least two fragments. Group medians; descriptive.
